learning_objective: The learner will classify each of twelve accessibility requirements under the WCAG principle it belongs to (perceivable, operable, understandable, or robust), with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** wcag-principles-sorter
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify each of twelve accessibility requirements under the WCAG principle it belongs to (perceivable, operable, understandable, or robust), with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Accessibility, WCAG (both defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each requirement the learner commits one of four principles. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct principle column in Content. Mastery is at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Reading the principle definitions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Captions belong under Understandable because they explain speech. (2) Contrast is Operable because users act on the page. (3) All requirements about HTML are Robust. **Instructional Rationale:** Classifying requirements under the four principles is an Understand-level action that shows the learner how the long list of criteria is organized. Three requirements per principle, each tied to a different need, teach the learner to ask which kind of barrier a requirement removes. **Content:** The four principles: Perceivable (users can sense the content), Operable (users can control it), Understandable (users can follow it), Robust (it works with assistive technology). The twelve requirements: | # | Requirement shown to the learner | Correct principle | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Images have text alternatives. | Perceivable | A user who cannot see needs another way to perceive it. | | 2 | Video with sound has captions. | Perceivable | A user who cannot hear needs another way to perceive it. | | 3 | Text has enough contrast with its background. | Perceivable | A user with low vision must be able to see it. | | 4 | Every function can be used with a keyboard. | Operable | A user who cannot use a mouse must be able to control it. | | 5 | Users can pause or stop moving content. | Operable | Users must be able to control content that moves. | | 6 | Users can see which element has keyboard focus. | Operable | A keyboard user must see where they are in order to operate the page. | | 7 | The language of the page is identified. | Understandable | Tools and users need to know which language the text is in. | | 8 | Navigation is consistent from page to page. | Understandable | Users can follow a page when its navigation behaves as before. | | 9 | Form errors are described in text. | Understandable | Users must be able to understand what went wrong and how to fix it. | | 10 | Custom buttons expose a name and a role to assistive technology. | Robust | Assistive technology must be able to read and operate them. | | 11 | Status messages can be announced without moving focus. | Robust | Assistive technology must be able to report them. | | 12 | The content works with a range of browsers and assistive technologies. | Robust | The content must not depend on one tool. | **Provenance:** The principles and the requirements follow the chapter section "WCAG", and each requirement paraphrases a criterion of WCAG 2.1. The sim states that the wording is simplified and names the WCAG documents as the authority. **Rules:** Each requirement has exactly one correct principle, three per principle. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one requirement and the four principles. 2. The learner may open the principle definitions. Opening them does not change the score. 3. The learner places the requirement under a principle, and the placement is committed. 4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text. 5. After requirement 12 the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 12 requirements in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [principle]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [principle]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 12 correct on the first attempt". At 10 or more it adds "You can sort the WCAG requirements." Below 10 it lists the Why text of each missed requirement. **Starting State:** The first requirement, the four principles, and the definitions closed. The question shown is "Which principle does this requirement serve?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter says the four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, abbreviated POUR, and that the levels are A, AA, and AAA.
